title: Fewer things
hook: owning less, as the forest monks do
tomorrow: can wanting less turn into one more thing to want?

segments.voice: That was the week of keeping going: the long view, joy that belongs, gladness for others, and yesterday's line, lightly. Ikkyu's broken cup: whatever comes together comes apart.

Moving boxes have a way of asking a question: do I really need all this? Mai's grandfather, Ông Thanh, is asking it this week. We met an old monk on the day about ageing well who got the opposite offer. Today, look again, this time at what he owned. Mahakassapa was old, and he wore heavy robes stitched from cast-off rags. The Buddha said to him, in paraphrase: Kassapa, you're old now, and those rag robes must weigh on you. Wear robes that householders give, accept their invitations to meals, and stay near me. It was a kind offer from his teacher, and Kassapa said no.
screen: `DO I REALLY NEED ALL THIS?` → `OLD KASSAPA, IN RAG ROBES.` → `THE BUDDHA OFFERS COMFORT.` → `KASSAPA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: He told the Buddha why. For a long time he had lived in the forest, eaten only what came to his bowl, worn rag robes, kept just three robes. He saw two reasons to keep going. It was a pleasant way to live, here and now. And he felt compassion for those who would come later: they might follow his example. The Buddha said: good, good, Kassapa. Keep your rag robes. That's the teaching under fewer things. Monks in the Buddha's order own little on purpose: robes, a bowl, a few needed things, and food that comes as a gift. Kassapa kept the stricter forest practices, the dhutangas, and forest monks today still take some of them up, freely. Not to punish the body; the Buddha turned away from that road in his first teaching. Fewer things means fewer things to guard, and an example for whoever is watching. Now the week, gathered up. Sumedha took the long view, face down in the mud. Bhaddiya, with nothing left to guard, cried what bliss. The Buddha was glad for Kondañña. Ikkyu handed back a broken cup. Each one loosened a grip: on time, on a palace, on credit, on a cup.
screen: `TWO REASONS: EASE NOW, AND LATER ONES.` · `GOOD, GOOD, KASSAPA.` · `FEWER THINGS TO GUARD.` · `THE WEEK: MUD, TREE, CRY, CUP.` · then, large: `FEWER THINGS.`

segments.voice: Pick up one thing within reach that you own: a pen, a mug, a book. Hold it and look at it the way Kassapa might, as something you need or something you guard. Then set it down, rest your hands empty in your lap, and sit. Notice how little the hands need to hold for the next two minutes.
Fewer things: owning little on purpose, like Kassapa in his rag robes. For an easier life now, and for whoever comes after.
Your line: fewer things, and fewer things to guard. A week of keeping going, done.

chat.meaning: Old Kassapa kept his rag robes by choice: ease now and an example for later generations. The Buddha said: good, good.

tie.story: The Buddha offered old Kassapa softer robes; Kassapa kept his rag robes, for ease now and for those who'd come after.
